items.followUp: How does electronegativity change down a group and across a period?

rubric.why: Checks the trend down a group.
rubric.description: States that electropositivity increases down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct downward trend in a group.

rubric.why: Checks the trend across a period.
rubric.description: States that electropositivity decreases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct trend across a period.

modelAnswer: Electropositivity increases down a group.
Electropositivity decreases from left to right across a period.

items.followUp: What happens to the temperature of a solution when dissolution is exothermic, and why?

rubric.why: Assesses how heat is released during dissolution.
rubric.description: Explains that forming attractions between solute and solvent particles releases heat.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking solute–solvent attraction formation with heat release.

rubric.why: Assesses the effect of the released heat.
rubric.description: States that the solution warms up or that the dissolution is exothermic.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that heat is released and the solution temperature rises.

modelAnswer: When solute and solvent particles form attractions, heat may be released.
If more heat is released than absorbed during dissolution, the process is exothermic and the solution temperature rises.

items.followUp: Give two differences between a suspension and a colloid.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the particle sizes in a colloid and a true solution.
rubric.description: States that colloid particles are larger than solution particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct particle-size comparison.

rubric.description: Gives a correct distinguishing property, such as the Tyndall effect or settling behaviour.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid difference other than particle size.

modelAnswer: A true solution has very small solute particles, whereas colloidal particles are larger.
A true solution does not scatter light, whereas a colloid scatters light and shows the Tyndall effect.

rubric.why: Checks what the mass-to-volume concentration represents.
rubric.description: Defines m/v as the mass of solute in a stated volume of solution, conventionally 100 mL.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct mass of solute per 100 mL of solution.

rubric.why: Checks the concentration relationship or formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for % m/v = (mass of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100, with compatible units.

modelAnswer: m/v means mass by volume concentration.
% m/v = (mass of solute in grams ÷ volume of solution in millilitres) × 100.
It represents the grams of solute present in 100 mL of solution.

items.followUp: What is rusting? Give one condition necessary for it to occur.

rubric.description: Defines corrosion as the gradual damage or deterioration of a metal by its surroundings.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition referring to metal deterioration or damage.

rubric.why: Checks that the student can give a relevant example.
rubric.description: Gives rusting of iron as an example of corrosion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the example of iron rusting.

modelAnswer: Corrosion is the gradual destruction or deterioration of a metal by chemical reactions with its environment.
Rusting of iron is an example of corrosion.

items.followUp: Define an alloy and give one example made from copper.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of an alloy.
rubric.description: Defines an alloy as a mixture of two or more elements, including a metal and another element or elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as a mixture of two or more elements, with at least one being a metal.

rubric.why: Checks for a valid example and its constituents.
rubric.description: Gives a valid alloy example, such as brass (copper and zinc) or bronze (copper and tin).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example; naming its constituents also earns this mark.

modelAnswer: An alloy is a mixture of two or more elements, at least one of which is a metal.
Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, is an example.

items.followUp: Name two metals added to iron to make stainless steel and state one property of stainless steel.

rubric.why: Checks the main constituents of stainless steel.
rubric.description: Identifies stainless steel as an iron alloy containing chromium and usually nickel.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for iron with chromium and nickel; accept an equivalent correct statement of its composition.

rubric.why: Checks the characteristic property that distinguishes stainless steel.
rubric.description: States that stainless steel resists corrosion or rusting.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct corrosion-resistance property.

modelAnswer: Stainless steel is an alloy of iron containing chromium and usually nickel.
It is resistant to corrosion and rusting.

items.followUp: Give three differences between Rutherford’s and Bohr’s atomic theories.

rubric.why: Checks the difference in the permitted electron orbits or energy levels.
rubric.description: Contrasts Rutherford’s unrestricted orbits with Bohr’s fixed, allowed orbits or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast about permitted orbits or energy levels.

rubric.why: Checks the theories’ treatment of electron energy and radiation.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model does not provide stable non-radiating orbits, whereas Bohr’s stationary orbits do not radiate energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast about radiation or energy loss.

rubric.why: Checks the consequence for atomic stability.
rubric.description: Contrasts the instability implied by Rutherford’s model with the stability of Bohr’s model.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast about atomic stability.

rubric.why: Checks the explanatory power of the two models.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model cannot explain the hydrogen line spectrum, whereas Bohr’s model explains it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison about the hydrogen spectrum.

rubric.why: Checks Bohr’s explanation of spectral lines through changes in electron energy.
rubric.description: Explains that Bohr’s model accounts for spectral lines through electron transitions between energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking electron transitions between energy levels to Bohr’s explanation of spectra.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s theory allows electrons to revolve around the nucleus in any orbit; Bohr’s theory allows electrons only in certain fixed orbits or energy levels.
In Rutherford’s model, an accelerating electron should radiate energy; in Bohr’s model, an electron in a stationary allowed orbit does not radiate energy.
Rutherford’s model therefore implies that electrons lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, making the atom unstable; Bohr’s model accounts for stable atoms.
Rutherford’s theory cannot explain the line spectrum of hydrogen; Bohr’s theory explains the hydrogen spectrum.
Bohr explained spectral lines by proposing that electrons absorb or emit definite amounts of energy when they jump between allowed energy levels.
